newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Won for the World Bank.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Won for the World Bank.

text.p: The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development launched the first-ever Korean won bond into international markets on Friday.
The IBRD, or World Bank, also launched a domestic tranche.
The 95 billion won issue was split as 71.5 billion worth for the South Korean domestic market and 23.5 billion for the overseas market.
Daewoo Securities is lead manager.
The bond for overseas consumption is due in 2002. It has a semi-annual coupon of 9.8 percent and was priced at par to give an annual yield of 10.04 percent, bankers in Hong Kong said.

The group for the overseas issue comprises Daewoo Securities, ING Barings, HSBC Markets, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, Oakreed Financial Services, Tokyo-Mitsubishi Bank, Union Bank of Switzerland and Yamaichi.
"The issue should appeal to any investor that is interested in building up a portfolio of various Asian currencies but does not want to take local credit risk," said a syndicate manager.
The World Bank is rated AAA.
The deal is expected to attract the same sort of emerging market funds that took an interest in the recent collection of Philippine peso-denominated Eurobonds launched by AAA-rated supranationals.
The World Bank, the International Finance Corp and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development launched peso bonds in March.
The World Bank won issue will be signed on April 14. The payment date is April 23, 1997.
The EBRD plans to launch a similar won-denominated issue that will be signed on April 21, Korea's finance ministry said.
In other news, Bank of China signed its US$300 million floating rate note issue.

Zhang Guo Wen, executive vice president and managing director at Bank of China's head office, said that the strong market response to the issue reflected international investors' support for China as well as for Bank of China, the leading state-owned commercial bank.
Oliver Jury, vice president at joint lead manager Morgan Stanley International, said about 60 percent of the Bank of China note issue placed in Asia, with the remainder sold to European investors.
Since the notes have been free to trade, the price has improved to 99.88 from 99.80 at launch, he said.
Bank of China's Zhang said the bank is likely to raise funds again "but when, in what currency and with what instrument will depend on our funding requirements and capital market conditions."
Proceeds of the US$300 million floating rate note will be used to partially finance energy exploration, Zhang said.
Thailand launched its Yankee overnight and managed to sell US$600 million in bonds. As expected, it scrapped the idea of a 30-year tranche and sold 10-year bonds only.
The 7.750 percent bonds were priced at 99.603 to yield 7.808 percent, or 90 basis points over comparable Treasuries.
Bankers in Hong Kong called the bond a success, noting that the pricing was reasonable following Thailand's downgrade by Moody's Investors Service this week.
Thai officials and analysts also said they were pleased with the deal's pricing given the ratings cut and the uncertain interest rate environment in the U.S.
